Pilling.deeper: Gintis and Mead described pilling as overlapping stages: abrasion draws loose fiber ends to the surface as fuzz, rubbing entangles that fuzz into pills once its density reaches a critical level, and further abrasion eventually breaks the anchoring fibers so pills wear off. Visible pill count is a balance of formation and loss. Interfiber friction and bending stiffness influence fuzz formation; fiber fineness, cross-sectional shape and stiffness influence entanglement; tenacity and flex-abrasion resistance govern wear-off, so strong polyester fibers can hold pills that weaker fibers would shed. Standard tests accelerate this: ISO 12945-1 tumbles specimens in a rotating pill box, ISO 12945-2 rubs them against a standard abradant in a modified Martindale tester, and ISO 12945-3 and ASTM D3512 use random tumbling. Specimens are rated against photographic references from 5 (no change) to 1 (very severe). ASTM D3512 is harsher than the ISO tumble method and not directly comparable.
Pilling.origins: A widely cited analysis of the process is Gintis and Mead, 'The Mechanism of Pilling', Textile Research Journal, 1959. The pill box method now in ISO 12945-1 derives from an apparatus developed at Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI). The Martindale tester dates to 1942, when James Graham Martindale of the Wool Industries Research Association in the UK was asked to test carbon-impregnated cloth intended to protect against gas; workshop head Stanley Dilworth built the first machine and James H. Heal manufactured it. Its rubbing path traces Lissajous figures, named after the French physicist Jules A. Lissajous.

Post-consumer.deeper: Post-consumer feedstock is heterogeneous, and its composition limits what recycling can do. A study of 2,173 kg of textiles (9,333 items) donated to Canadian thrift stores found about 55 percent suitable for immediate resale and 24 percent needing repair or cleaning; cotton was the dominant fiber at 50.2 percent of items and polyester followed at 29.2 percent, with many blends containing small amounts of spandex that can contaminate recycling streams. A Norwegian dataset documents 16,464 garments (4,157 kg) to support such estimates. Sorting increasingly relies on near-infrared spectroscopy with machine-learning classifiers to separate cotton, nylon and polyester. Recovery then diverges: mechanical opening shortens fibers, while polymer or pulp routes such as recycled cotton pulp for lyocell or viscose rebuild material. Bottle-derived polyester is also post-consumer, but it recycles packaging rather than closing a textile loop.
Post-consumer.origins: Distinguishing used from unused recycled material has a long legal history in wool. The US Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 grouped reclaimed fiber into one 'recycled wool' category covering both unused manufactured products and products a consumer had used, reflecting a trade concern with shoddy. Voluntary standards and the FTC Green Guides later framed recycled-content claims around recovery from the waste stream. In the EU, the Waste Framework Directive requires separate collection of textile waste from 2025, which is driving the new data on post-consumer composition.

Pre-consumer.deeper: Pre-consumer streams include cutting-room offcuts, yarn and spinning waste, and finishing waste, and each behaves differently. A 2026 study of rotor yarns found that droppings from spinning blended with cotton with limited quality loss, whereas brush fiber shed during sueding or emerizing of dyed fabric gave acceptable yarns with higher mass irregularity, imperfections and hairiness, because its fibers were shorter; the waste did, however, supply color without further dyeing. Because such streams are clean and well characterized, they also suit non-textile uses: one company's post-industrial cotton patches were shredded into fibers of at most 35 mm, pretreated with alkaline mercerization wastewater and enzymatically hydrolyzed, recovering about 90 percent of the glucose for fermentation to lactic acid. The authors cite estimates that, globally, less than 1 percent of textile waste is recycled back into new garments.
Pre-consumer.origins: The prefix marks when the waste arises relative to the consumer. Older US wool law blurred the line, since the 1939 Wool Products Labeling Act placed unused manufactured products and used goods in a single 'recycled wool' category. Voluntary standards later separated the two and debated which manufacturing scrap qualifies. Commercial textile-to-textile recycling often started with pre-consumer material: Lenzing states that its REFIBRA technology, introduced in 2017, first used cotton cutting waste before adding post-consumer textiles.

Regenerated cellulose.deeper: Cellulose decomposes before it melts, because of its dense hydrogen-bonding network, so it must be dissolved and spun from solution; regeneration converts it largely from the native cellulose I crystal form to cellulose II. Three chemistries dominate. In viscose, pulp steeped in sodium hydroxide reacts with carbon disulfide to form cellulose xanthate, which dissolves in dilute alkali and regenerates in a sulfuric acid bath. In lyocell, pulp dissolves directly in aqueous N-methylmorpholine N-oxide and is spun across an air gap; Lenzing states that more than 99.8 percent of the solvent is recovered. Cupro uses Schweizer's reagent, a tetraamminecopper(II) hydroxide solution. Wet strength separates them: one comparison reports lyocell at about 32 cN/tex dry and 29 wet, while viscose loses close to half. Worker exposure to carbon disulfide is the viscose route's documented hazard; one Taiwanese study found ECG abnormalities in 25.9 percent of exposed workers against 2.7 percent of controls.
Regenerated cellulose.origins: In 1857 the Swiss chemist Matthias Eduard Schweizer found that cotton dissolves in a solution of copper salts in ammonia and can be regenerated from it. Louis-Henri Despeissis patented spinning fibers from such solutions in 1890, and by 1891 Max Fremery and Johann Urban were making filaments by this route near Aachen; Bemberg artificial silk followed from 1908. Direct-solvent lyocell came much later, brought to commercial scale by Courtaulds, and in 1996 the US Federal Trade Commission recognized lyocell as a subclass of rayon.
